Q302.L1t: Prime factorization expresses every integer greater than 1 as a product of primes, and a factor of a number is any integer that divides it evenly.
Q302.L2t: Whether a number must be divisible by a given integer depends on whether all of that integer's prime factors, with their multiplicities, are guaranteed to appear in the number.
Q302.L3t: The listed primes each appear at least once, but nothing says any prime is repeated, and a factor that needs a prime not on the list, or a repeated prime, cannot be guaranteed.
Q302.L4t: The number must be divisible by ten, because both of its prime factors, two and five, are guaranteed to appear in it.
Q302.L2f: A number whose prime factors are listed is always divisible by every prime on the list raised to the second power, since each prime must appear at least twice.
Q302.L3f: Since the number is even, its smallest prime factor must appear at least twice, so the number is always divisible by the square of that prime.
Q302.L4f: The number must be divisible by four.

Q637.L1t: The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency of a wave when the source or the observer moves relative to the medium carrying the wave.
Q637.L2t: An echo from a stationary wall involves two Doppler shifts: the wall acts as an observer of the moving source, then as a stationary source re-emitting the received frequency toward the moving driver.
Q637.L3t: The wall receives a frequency of 600 × 350/346.5, about 606 Hz, and then re-emits that frequency toward the driver, who is moving toward it, so the received frequency is multiplied again by 353.5/350.
Q637.L4t: After both shifts the driver hears the echo at about 612 Hz.
Q637.L2f: The Doppler shift for sound depends only on the ratio of the source speed to the speed of sound and does not depend on whether the observer is moving.
Q637.L3f: Only the shift at the wall matters, because the reflected sound travels back to the driver at the wall's received frequency, and the driver's own motion adds no further change.
Q637.L4f: The driver hears the echo at about 606 Hz.

Q663.L1t: Counting problems about random assignments of items to positions are solved by comparing the number of favorable arrangements with the total number of equally likely arrangements.
Q663.L2t: There are 4! = 24 equally likely ways to deliver four distinct packages to four houses, one per house, and a derangement is an arrangement in which no item is in its correct place.
Q663.L3t: Choosing which two houses get the right package can be done in 6 ways, and the other two packages must then both be wrong, which for just two items can happen in only one way (they are swapped).
Q663.L4t: Six of the 24 equally likely arrangements have exactly two correct deliveries, so the probability is one quarter.
Q663.L2f: Each package independently has a one-in-four chance of reaching its correct house, so the number of correct deliveries follows a binomial distribution with four trials.
Q663.L3f: Because each of the four packages independently lands at the right house with probability one fourth, the chance that exactly two do is 6 × (1/4)² × (3/4)².
Q663.L4f: The probability is twenty-seven over one hundred twenty-eight.
